Dear Editor,

Please consider our manuscript, *Insurance coverage, service use, and payment at outpatient contact among adults with disability in Kenya before the SHA transition: a secondary analysis of KDHS 2022*, for publication as a Research Article.

Using the KDHS 2022 person recode, we measure disability with the Washington Group Short Set and describe insurance coverage, outpatient and inpatient service use, and payment at the last outpatient contact among 40,197 adults. Three results carry the paper. Adults meeting the disability threshold were more likely to be uninsured than adults below it, unadjusted and after adjustment for sex, age group and residence (PR 1.10, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.13; a standardised difference of 6.7 percentage points), but the association was null once wealth and education were added, which indicates that the coverage deficit runs through economic position rather than alongside it. Their higher use of care did not behave that way and survived every specification (outpatient APR 1.63, 95% CI 1.52 to 1.74; hospitalisation APR 2.15, 95% CI 1.88 to 2.46). And at the point of care, among insured adults with disability who paid, an insurer met any part of the bill in 15.1% of cases, with a mean cash share of 86%.

That third result rests on the KDHS cost and payer variables rather than on a yes-or-no payment indicator, which is what allows the paper to say something about financial protection rather than about payment incidence alone. We report the amount paid, the part met out of pocket and the payer split, and we state explicitly that catastrophic expenditure cannot be constructed from these data because KDHS collects no consumption measure.

The timing matters. Kenya replaced the National Hospital Insurance Fund with the Social Health Authority on 1 October 2024, so KDHS 2022 is the last nationally representative measurement before the transition and cannot be re-collected. The Social Health Insurance Act 2023 routes support for households unable to pay through means testing rather than through a disability category, and our results speak directly to whether an enrolment-based monitoring framework would detect a change in what households actually pay.

The manuscript is original, is not under consideration elsewhere, and uses authorised de-identified survey microdata obtained from The DHS Program under an approved request. Analysis code is public. All authors have approved the submission and declare no competing interests.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Nichodemus Werre Amollo
